prompt: Write an essay on whether people learn more from failure or from success.
text:
# Learning from Failure and Success

People often say that failure is the best teacher. The claim is half true. Failure teaches vividly, but success teaches things that failure cannot, and neither teaches much unless the learner reflects on it.

The case for failure is strong. When something goes wrong, you get clear evidence that your approach was flawed. A bridge collapses, an experiment gives the wrong result, or a business loses customers, and each event forces a question: what did we get wrong? Failure also breaks assumptions. A person who succeeds can keep believing in a plan that worked by luck, while a person who fails has to look at the plan again. The emotional sting helps too. We remember painful mistakes longer than easy wins, and that memory shapes later choices.

Failure also exposes the edges of what we know. A student who fails an exam learns which topics she misunderstood. A chess player who loses learns which patterns he missed. These lessons are specific and hard to get any other way, because success rarely shows you where your knowledge runs out.

But failure has limits as a teacher. It tells you that something went wrong, and often not why. A startup may fail because of its product, its timing, its team, or plain bad luck, and the founders may draw the wrong conclusion from any of these. Failure can also discourage. Someone who fails repeatedly with no progress may learn only that they are bad at the task, which is a lesson that is both false and harmful. And failure is a poor guide to what to do next. Knowing that one path leads nowhere does not tell you which path leads somewhere.

Success fills that gap. When something works, you learn what to repeat. You see which skills, habits, and conditions produce results, and you can build on them. Success also builds confidence, which makes people willing to attempt harder problems. Much of expertise comes from this: a surgeon, a pianist, or a programmer improves by practicing a technique correctly many times until it becomes automatic. Doing something right teaches the correct form, and doing it wrong cannot.

Success has its own risk, which is that it teaches too little. A win can hide weak points, and people tend to credit their skill and ignore luck. A company that grows quickly in a booming market may conclude that its strategy is brilliant, and then fail when conditions change. Because success feels good, people rarely examine it, and so they miss what it could show them.

The better question is what makes either experience instructive. The answer is analysis. A person who studies a failure carefully, asking what happened, why, and what they would change, learns far more than one who just feels bad and moves on. The same is true of success. Asking why something worked, and whether it would work again, turns a lucky result into usable knowledge. Fields that learn fast, such as aviation and medicine, do this on purpose. They review crashes and near misses, but they also study routine flights and procedures that went well.

The size of the experience matters as well. Small failures are the most useful, since they are cheap and give quick feedback. A child learning to walk falls hundreds of times and loses nothing. Catastrophic failures teach a lot but cost too much, and many who suffer them never get to apply the lesson. The best learning happens when people can fail often at low stakes and succeed often enough to stay motivated.

So neither failure nor success is the better teacher in general. Failure is better at correcting mistakes and showing the limits of our understanding. Success is better at confirming what works and building skill and confidence. A person who only fails gets discouraged, and a person who only succeeds grows complacent. The people who learn most are those who seek a mix of both and who take the time to ask what each one means.
